claim: Dravet Syndrome is an intractable form of childhood epilepsy associated with deleterious mutations in SCN1A, the gene encoding neuronal sodium channel Nav1.1.
source: Dravet Syndrome is an intractable form of childhood epilepsy associated with deleterious mutations in SCN1A, the gene encoding neuronal sodium channel Nav1.1.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The p.S1328P mutation in Nav1.1 was identified in a pair of twins with Dravet Syndrome.
source: We studied a Nav1.1 mutation (p.S1328P) identified in a pair of twins with Dravet Syndrome and generated iPSC-derived neurons from these patients.
evidence: The manuscript describes obtaining fibroblasts from twins and sequencing revealed the mutation, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The p.S1328P mutation causes a decrease in Nav1.1 current amplitude.
source: Characterization of the mutant channel revealed a decrease in current amplitude and hypersensitivity to steady-state inactivation.
evidence: Experimental data from patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 1D and Table 1 demonstrate reduced current amplitude.

claim: The p.S1328P mutation causes hypersensitivity to steady-state inactivation.
source: Characterization of the mutant channel revealed a decrease in current amplitude and hypersensitivity to steady-state inactivation.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Table 2 demonstrate a hyperpolarizing shift in steady-state inactivation voltage.

claim: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in sodium currents.
source: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in sodium currents and action potential firing, which were rescued by a Nav1.1 transgene, whereas Dravet excitatory neurons were normal.
evidence: Patch clamp data in Figure 4E-F and Table 3 show reduced sodium current amplitude in Dravet inhibitory neurons.

claim: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in action potential firing.
source: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in sodium currents and action potential firing, which were rescued by a Nav1.1 transgene, whereas Dravet excitatory neurons were normal.
evidence: Current clamp recordings in Figure 5E-H demonstrate reduced firing frequency and altered input-output relationships in Dravet inhibitory neurons.

claim: The deficits in Dravet inhibitory neurons were rescued by a Nav1.1 transgene.
source: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in sodium currents and action potential firing, which were rescued by a Nav1.1 transgene, whereas Dravet excitatory neurons were normal.
evidence: Figure 6D and 6F show that Nav1.1 cDNA expression restored sodium currents and action potential firing in Dravet inhibitory neurons.

claim: Dravet excitatory neurons were normal.
source: Dravet inhibitory neurons showed deficits in sodium currents and action potential firing, which were rescued by a Nav1.1 transgene, whereas Dravet excitatory neurons were normal.
evidence: Figure 4C-D and Figure 5A-D show no significant differences between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in sodium currents or action potential firing.

claim: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SCN1A gene are the most common genetic basis for Dravet Syndrome.
source: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SCN1A gene are the most common genetic basis for Dravet Syndrome (Catterall et al., 2010; Escayg and Goldin, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCN1A encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1.
source: SCN1A encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, which contributes the fast depolarization of neuronal membranes during an action potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Nav1.1 contributes the fast depolarization of neuronal membranes during an action potential.
source: SCN1A encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, which contributes the fast depolarization of neuronal membranes during an action potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of voltage-gated sodium channels.

claim: Loss of one copy of Scn1a impaired the excitability of hippocampal inhibitory interneurons but not excitatory neurons in a mouse model of Dravet Syndrome.
source: Initial insights into the neurobiological function of Nav1.1 came from studies of a mouse model of Dravet Syndrome, where the loss of one copy of Scn1a impaired the excitability of hippocampal inhibitory interneurons but not excitatory neurons (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2006.

claim: The disproportionate contribution of Nav1.1 to the excitability of inhibitory interneurons in the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum and thalamus was confirmed by additional studies.
source: The disproportionate contribution of Nav1.1 to the excitability of inhibitory interneurons in the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum and thalamus was confirmed by additional studies (Cheah et al., 2012; Dutton et al., 2012; Kalume et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2010; Ogiwara et al., 2007, 2013; Tai et al., 2014; Tsai et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The effect of the Nav1.1 mutation in the mouse is dependent on the genetic background with seizures occurring in the C57/B6 background but absent in the 129 background.
source: but the effect of the Nav1.1 mutation in the mouse is dependent on the genetic background with seizures occurring in the C57/B6 background but absent in the 129 background (Mistry et al., 2014; Ogiwara et al., 2007; Rubinstein et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The Serine-1328 residue is located in a voltage-sensing transmembrane segment of the Nav1.1 protein.
source: The Serine-1328 residue is located in a voltage-sensing transmembrane segment of the protein, and it is conserved in human and mouse Nav1.1 α subunits.
evidence: Figure 1A shows the location of the mutation in Domain III Transmembrane Segment 4 (DIII-S4).

claim: The Serine-1328 residue is conserved in human and mouse Nav1.1 α subunits.
source: The Serine-1328 residue is located in a voltage-sensing transmembrane segment of the protein, and it is conserved in human and mouse Nav1.1 α subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on sequence analysis.

claim: The p.S1328P mutation has previously been described in other individuals with Dravet Syndrome.
source: This mutation has previously been described in other individuals with Dravet Syndrome (SCN1A Infobase: http://www.scn1a.info/; SCN1A variant database: http://www.molgen.ua.ac.be/scn1amutations/) but the functional effects of the mutation are not known.
evidence: This is supported by references to mutation databases.

claim: The p.F383S mutation makes the Nav1.1 channel resistant to tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: To distinguish the exogenous from the endogenous channels we introduced a second mutation, p.F383S, that makes the channel resistant to tetrodotoxin (TTX).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cestèle et al., 2008, 2013 and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nav1.1-F383S and Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P were expressed at similar levels in NgN2 neurons.
source: We found that Nav1.1-F383S and Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P were expressed at similar levels in NgN2 neurons following treatment with either 0.1 µg/ml or 2 µg/ml Dox in the culture media (Figure 1C), suggesting that the mutation does not affect the expression of the channel.
evidence: Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C demonstrates similar protein expression levels.

claim: The S1328P mutation does not affect the expression of the Nav1.1 channel.
source: We found that Nav1.1-F383S and Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P were expressed at similar levels in NgN2 neurons following treatment with either 0.1 µg/ml or 2 µg/ml Dox in the culture media (Figure 1C), suggesting that the mutation does not affect the expression of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blotting data showing similar expression levels.

claim: Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P produces currents that are significantly smaller than those of control channels.
source: We found that Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P produces currents that are significantly smaller than those of control channels when the cells are treated with both 0.1 µg/ml and 2 µg/ml Dox (Figure 1D and Table 1).
evidence: Patch clamp data in Figure 1D and Table 1 show statistically significant reduction in current amplitude (p = 0.0308).

claim: The S1328P mutation affects either the number of channels on the cell surface or the activity of the Nav1.1 channel.
source: This suggests that the S1328P either affects the number of channels on the cell surface or the activity of the Nav1.1 channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced currents despite similar total expression levels.

claim: There is a defect in trafficking the S1328P mutant channel to the cell surface.
source: The trend that the current observed in the presence of 2 µg/ml Dox was larger than that observed in the presence of 0.1 µg/ml Dox in the cells expressing the mutant channels but not the control channels suggests that there is a defect in trafficking the channel to the cell surfaces (Figure 1D and Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent increase in current for mutant but not control channels.

claim: The activation voltage (V1/2) of Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P was hyperpolarized by around 5 mV.
source: The activation voltage (V1/2) was hyperpolarized by around 5 mV, while the steady-state inactivation voltage (V1/2') showed a hyperpolarizing shift of around 15 mV (Figure 1E and Table 2).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 1E and Table 2 show V1/2 values of -30.22 mV for control and -35.35 mV for mutant (p = 0.0324).

claim: The steady-state inactivation voltage (V1/2') of Nav1.1-F383S-S1328P showed a hyperpolarizing shift of around 15 mV.
source: The activation voltage (V1/2) was hyperpolarized by around 5 mV, while the steady-state inactivation voltage (V1/2') showed a hyperpolarizing shift of around 15 mV (Figure 1E and Table 2).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 1E and Table 2 show V1/2' values of -46.23 mV for control and -61.43 mV for mutant (p = 1.6 × 10−12).

claim: The increased sensitivity for activation is likely to enhance the activity of the channel in neurons slightly.
source: This increased sensitivity for activation is likely to enhance the activity of the channel in neurons slightly, however, the much larger increase in steady-state inactivation offsets this effect and probably results in a net loss of function by reducing the fraction of channels that are available to open under prolonged current injections.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biophysical data.

claim: The much larger increase in steady-state inactivation offsets the effect of increased activation sensitivity and probably results in a net loss of function.
source: This increased sensitivity for activation is likely to enhance the activity of the channel in neurons slightly, however, the much larger increase in steady-state inactivation offsets this effect and probably results in a net loss of function by reducing the fraction of channels that are available to open under prolonged current injections.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the biophysical properties measured.

claim: Six iPSC lines were generated from the Dravet Syndrome twins carrying the heterozygous p.S1328P mutation in Nav1.1.
source: We next generated six iPSC lines from the Dravet Syndrome twins carrying the heterozygous p.S1328P mutation in Nav1.1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The methods section describes the generation of these cell lines.

claim: Episomal vectors expressing SOX2, OCT3/4, L-MYC, KLF4, LIN28, and p53-shRNA were used to convert skin fibroblasts into iPSCs.
source: We converted skin fibroblasts from the patients into iPSCs using episomal vectors expressing SOX2, OCT3/4, L-MYC, KLF4, LIN28, and p53-shRNA as described previously (Okita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the methods and supported by citation to Okita et al., 2011.

claim: The reprogramming vectors were lost in most iPSC cell lines after the 15th passage.
source: We used RT-PCR to verify that the reprogramming vectors were lost in most iPSC cell lines after the 15th passage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B demonstrates loss of episomal vector transcripts.

claim: The iPSC lines expressed the pluripotency markers NANOG, TRA-2-49, OCT3/4 SOX2, and LIN28.
source: The iPSC lines expressed the pluripotency markers NANOG, TRA-2-49, OCT3/4 SOX2, and LIN28 (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry and qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3 show expression of these markers.

claim: Four of the iPSC lines responded well to neural differentiation, which was evident by the formation of neural rosettes.
source: Four of the iPSC lines responded well to neural differentiation, which was evident by the formation of neural rosettes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 show neural rosette formation.

claim: The iPSCs had between three and sixteen novel CNVs, all of which were less than 1.5 Mb in size.
source: The iPSCs had between three and sixteen novel CNVs, all of which were less than 1.5 Mb in size and none of which occurred in well annotated pathogenic regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: SNP array data analyzed for copy number variants as described in methods.

claim: None of the novel CNVs in the iPSCs occurred in well annotated pathogenic regions.
source: The iPSCs had between three and sixteen novel CNVs, all of which were less than 1.5 Mb in size and none of which occurred in well annotated pathogenic regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: SNP array analysis as described in methods and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The number of novel CNVs in each cell line was below the median number observed in a previous SNP array based characterization of reprogramming associated CNVs.
source: The number of novel CNVs in each cell line was below the median number observed in a previous SNP array based characterization of reprogramming associated CNVs (Hussein et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison is made to a published study by Hussein et al., 2011.

claim: Six iPSC lines were generated from 4 control subjects, 2 males and 2 females, none of whom had a diagnosis of epilepsy.
source: We also generated six iPSC lines derived from 4 control subjects, 2 males and 2 females, none of whom had a diagnosis of epilepsy.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The excitatory neuron differentiation protocol generates neural stem cells and progenitors that express FOXG1 and PAX6.
source: This protocol generates neural stem cells and progenitors that express FOXG1 and PAX6, two markers that are characteristic of telencephalic identity (Figure 2C, top)
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 2C shows expression of these markers.

claim: FOXG1 and PAX6 are markers that are characteristic of telencephalic identity.
source: This protocol generates neural stem cells and progenitors that express FOXG1 and PAX6, two markers that are characteristic of telencephalic identity (Figure 2C, top)
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental neuroscience.

claim: The excitatory neuron protocol generates cortical neurons that express layer-specific cortical markers including FOXP1, SATB2, CTIP2 and ETV1.
source: and cortical neurons that express layer-specific cortical markers including FOXP1, SATB2, CTIP2 and ETV1 (Paşca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The neural stem cells and progenitors generated using the ventral telencephalon patterning protocol co-expressed transcription factors NKX2.1, FOXG1 and OLIG2.
source: The neural stem cells and progenitors that were generated using the ventral telencephalon patterning protocol co-expressed transcription factors NKX2.1, FOXG1 and OLIG2 (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B)
evidence: Immunostaining and qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 show expression of these markers.

claim: NKX2.1, FOXG1 and OLIG2 together characterize the MGE region in the human embryonic brain.
source: which together characterize the MGE region in the human embryonic brain (Maroof et al., 2013; Nicholas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ventral telencephalon protocol cells also expressed LHX6, an MGE-specific transcription factor acting downstream of NKX2.1.
source: The cells also expressed LHX6 (Figure 2B), an MGE-specific transcription factor acting downstream of NKX2.1
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B shows LHX6 expression, and its role is established knowledge.

claim: The ventral telencephalon protocol cells expressed transcription factors GSH2 and DLX2 that cooperate in the development of ventral telencephalic structures including MGE.
source: as well as transcription factors GSH2 and DLX2 (Figure 2B) that cooperate in the development of ventral telencephalic structures including MGE (Wonders and Anderson, 2006).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B shows expression, and the role is supported by citation.

claim: PAX6 was downregulated in the ventral patterning protocol.
source: In contrast, PAX6, a transcription factor characteristic of dorsal telencephalic progenitors that form excitatory neurons (Toresson et al., 2000; Yun et al., 2001), was downregulated in the ventral patterning protocol (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: qRT-PCR and immunostaining data in Figure 2B and 2C show reduced PAX6 expression in ventral vs dorsal patterning.

claim: PAX6 is a transcription factor characteristic of dorsal telencephalic progenitors that form excitatory neurons.
source: In contrast, PAX6, a transcription factor characteristic of dorsal telencephalic progenitors that form excitatory neurons (Toresson et al., 2000; Yun et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ventral telencephalon protocol led to minimal expression of the transcription factors COUP-TFII and SP8.
source: Finally the protocol led to minimal expression of the transcription factors COUP-TFII and SP8 (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C show low expression of these markers.

claim: COUP-TFII is known to be expressed in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE), the dorsal portion of lateral ganglionic eminence (dLGE), and the dorsal portion of MGE (dMGE).
source: COUP-TFII is known to be expressed in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE), the dorsal portion of lateral ganglionic eminence (dLGE), and the dorsal portion of MGE (dMGE).
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental neuroscience.

claim: SP8 is largely co-expressed with COUP-TFII in the dorsal CGE (dCGE) and dLGE but absent from MGE.
source: SP8 is largely co-expressed with COUP-TFII in the dorsal CGE (dCGE) and dLGE but absent from MGE (Cai et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A large fraction of the neural stem cells and progenitors made using the ventral protocol have an MGE identity, while a small fraction have dLGE and/or CGE identity.
source: The strong induction of NKX2.1 and mild induction of COUP-TFII and SP8 suggest that a large fraction of the neural stem cells and progenitors made using this protocol have an MGE identity, while a small fraction of the cells have dLGE and/or CGE identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: About 30% of MAP2-positive neurons generated from the ventral telencephalic protocol were co-stained by an anti-GABA antibody.
source: Among all neurons that were identified by MAP2 staining, about 30% were co-stained by an anti-GABA antibody (Figure 3A), suggesting that they produce the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3A shows co-localization of MAP2 and GABA.

claim: Among the inhibitory (GABA+) neurons, approximately 50% co-expressed Calretinin.
source: Among the inhibitory (GABA+) neurons, approximately 50% co-expressed Calretinin, and 2%-8% expressed Somatostatin, and the rest expressed neither marker (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3C show these percentages.

claim: Among the inhibitory (GABA+) neurons, 2%-8% expressed Somatostatin.
source: Among the inhibitory (GABA+) neurons, approximately 50% co-expressed Calretinin, and 2%-8% expressed Somatostatin, and the rest expressed neither marker (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3C show these percentages.

claim: No cells expressing Parvalbumin were identified in the inhibitory neuron cultures.
source: We did not identify any cells that expressed Parvalbumin, possibly because these cells emerge during postnatal development and require both cell-intrinsic and non-intrinsic factors for specification, migration and maturation (Okaty et al., 2009; Sultan et al., 2013; Wonders and Anderson, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on immunostaining experiments, with speculation about the reason.

claim: Co-expression of NKX2.1 and Calretinin was observed in many cells with progenitor-like morphology and in a population of cells showing neuronal morphology.
source: We observed co-expression of NKX2.1 and Calretinin in many cells with progenitor-like morphology and also in a population of cells showing neuronal morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows co-localization.

claim: Expression of SP8 was barely detected in iPSC-derived inhibitory neurons.
source: Furthermore, expression of SP8, an aforementioned transcription factor found in CGE-derived progenitors and neurons, was barely detected in our iPSC-derived inhibitory neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B shows minimal SP8 expression.

claim: The Calretinin-expressing inhibitory neurons in this study originate from MGE-like progenitors.
source: These results are consistent with findings from the differentiating neural rosettes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and support the idea that the Calretinin-expressing inhibitory neurons in our study originate from MGE-like progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression of NKX2.1 with Calretinin and minimal SP8 expression.

claim: Approximately 65% of the Dlxi1/2b-GFP labeled neurons were co-stained by an anti-GABA antibody.
source: Approximately 65% of the Dlxi1/2b-GFP labeled neurons were co-stained by an anti-GABA antibody, indicating they are inhibitory neurons (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Immunostaining data in Figure 3D and quantification in Figure 3E show this percentage.

claim: About 70% of the Dlxi1/2b-GFP neurons expressed at least one of GAD65 or GAD67.
source: About 70% of the Dlxi1/2b-GFP neurons expressed at least one of the two markers, consistent with the results of the anti-GABA staining and independently of whether the neurons were derived from control or Dravet iPSCs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F demonstrates this percentage.

claim: Only a small percentage of GAD67/65-positive inhibitory neurons expressed 5HT3aR (0.9% of the control sample group and 5.4% of the Dravet group).
source: Furthermore, by single-cell RT-PCR only a small percentage of these GAD67/65-positive inhibitory neurons (0.9% of the control sample group and 5.4% of the Dravet group) expressed 5HT3aR, a serotonin receptor and specific marker for CGE-derived inhibitory interneurons
evidence: Single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 demonstrates these percentages.

claim: More than 60% of GAD67/65-positive inhibitory neurons expressed Calbindin (for both the control and Dravet groups).
source: while more than 60% (for both the control and Dravet groups) expressed Calbindin, which is commonly found in MGE-derived interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Single-cell RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 demonstrates this percentage.

claim: The cellular composition of the inhibitory neuron pool is dominated by MGE-like rather than CGE-like lineages.
source: These results are consistent with other characteristics of the neural differentiation protocol and indicate that the cellular composition of the inhibitory neuron pool is dominated by MGE-like rather than CGE-like lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the low expression of 5HT3aR and high expression of Calbindin.

claim: The fraction of inhibitory neurons firing continuous trains of action potentials increased as the cells matured at least until differentiation day 90.
source: The Inhibitory neurons fired trains of action potentials upon a 1000-millisecond current injection, and the fraction of cells firing continuous trains increased as the cells matured at least until differentiation day 90 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 3G shows maturation of firing patterns over time.

claim: At differentiation day 90, 73.3% of the inhibitory neurons showed an accommodating pattern of action potential firing.
source: At this later stage, 73.3% of the inhibitory neurons showed an accommodating pattern of action potential firing; 3.3% had a non-accommodating pattern; a 5% showed a stuttering pattern; and the remaining 18.4% fired at most a few or single action potentials (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Electrophysiological data summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 shows these percentages.

claim: Spontaneous inhibitory synaptic currents were observed that were blocked by Gabazine indicating that the cells have functional GABAergic synapses.
source: We also observed spontaneous inhibitory synaptic currents that were blocked by Gabazine indicating that the cells have functional GABAergic synapses (Figure 3H).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 3H shows Gabazine-sensitive currents.

claim: iPSC-derived inhibitory neurons engrafted into rat hippocampal organotypic slices formed functional inhibitory synapses with rat neurons.
source: Patch clamping of rat neurons surrounding the axons of ChR2-YFP-cells revealed light-driven Gabazine sensitive postsynaptic currents (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and E) indicating that the engrafted human inhibitory neurons formed synapses with the rat neurons.
evidence: Optogenetic and electrophysiological data in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 4 show functional synaptic transmission.

claim: There was no significant difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in sodium current amplitude.
source: When we measured INa in CaMKII-GFP-labeled telencephalic excitatory neurons, there was no significant difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in the amplitude (Figure 4C and D; Table 3)
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4C-D and Table 3 show p = 0.8225 by t-test.

claim: There was no significant difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in voltage dependence for activation.
source: there was no significant difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in the amplitude (Figure 4C and D; Table 3), voltage dependence for activation (Figure 4D and Table 3)
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4D and Table 3 show no significant difference in V1/2 (p = 0.3505).

claim: There was no significant difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in steady-state inactivation profile.
source: or steady-state inactivation profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Table 4).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Table 4 show p = 0.6551 by t-test.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the INa amplitude in Dlxi1/2b-GFP-labeled inhibitory neurons from individuals with Dravet Syndrome relative to controls.
source: In contrast, we observed a significant reduction in the INa amplitude in Dlxi1/2b-GFP-labeled inhibitory neurons from individuals with Dravet Syndrome relative to controls (p=0.034 by t-test; Figure 4E and F; Table 3).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4E-F and Table 3 show statistically significant reduction (p = 0.034).

claim: There were no significant differences between control and Dravet inhibitory neurons in the voltage dependence for INa activation.
source: There were no significant differences between control and Dravet inhibitory neurons in the voltage dependence for INa activation (Figure 4F; Table 3)
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4F and Table 3 show no significant difference in V1/2 (p = 0.2885).

claim: There were no significant differences between control and Dravet inhibitory neurons in the steady-state inactivation.
source: or the steady-state inactivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; Table 4).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Table 4 show p = 0.3035 by t-test.

claim: There was no statistical difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in the maximum frequency of action potential firing (fmax).
source: There was no statistical difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in the maximum frequency of action potential firing (fmax, Figure 5B)
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 5B shows p = 0.5115 by t-test.

claim: There was no statistical difference between control and Dravet excitatory neurons in the quantitative relationship between current injection and the number of action potentials that a cell fired (the dynamic output).
source: or in the quantitative relationship between current injection and the number of action potentials that a cell fired (the dynamic output, Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 5C-D shows p = 0.6015 by two-way ANOVA.

claim: There was a 40% reduction in the maximal firing frequency of inhibitory Dravet neurons compared to those in controls.
source: There was a 40% reduction in the maximal firing frequency of inhibitory Dravet neurons compared to those in controls (Figure 5E and F; p = 0.0154 by t-test).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 5E-F shows statistically significant reduction (p = 0.0006 as shown in figure, though text states p = 0.0154).

claim: At high current injection levels Dravet inhibitory neurons often fired only a few action potentials before entering depolarization block.
source: At high current injection levels Dravet inhibitory neurons often fired only a few action potentials before entering depolarization block, in contrast to the sustained trains of action potentials observed in the control neurons.
evidence: This is observed in the electrophysiological traces shown in Figure 5E and 5G.

claim: The input-output relationship of Dravet inhibitory neurons was bell shaped with reduced firing observed at high levels of stimulation.
source: Therefore, the input-output relationship of Dravet inhibitory neurons was bell shaped with reduced firing observed at high levels of stimulation (Figure 5G and H; between Dravet and control inhibitory neurons p<0.0001 by two way ANOVA, and p<0.05 by post hoc Sidak's multiple comparisons at the two highest stimulation levels).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 5G-H shows statistically significant differences.

claim: The loss of one copy of the Nav1.1 channels impairs the ability of inhibitory neurons from Dravet patients to fire at high frequencies.
source: This observation strongly suggests that the loss of one copy of the Nav1.1 channels impairs the ability of inhibitory neurons from Dravet patients to fire at high frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiological data showing reduced firing in Dravet inhibitory neurons.

claim: There was a 1.6–5.6 fold enrichment of Nav1.1 mRNA in cultures of inhibitory neurons relative to excitatory neurons derived from multiple control iPSC lines, Dravet iPSC lines and the hESC line H9.
source: When normalized to the expression of NaVβ3 mRNA, which encodes a sodium channel auxiliary subunit uniformly present among subtypes of mouse cortical neurons (Sugino et al., 2006), we observed a 1.6–5.6 fold enrichment of Nav1.1 mRNA in cultures of inhibitory neurons relative to excitatory neurons derived from multiple control iPSC lines, Dravet iPSC lines and the hESC line H9 (Figure 6A).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 6A shows this enrichment across multiple cell lines.

claim: Both Nav1.1 shRNAs reduced the expression of Nav1.1 mRNA by around 60%.
source: We first verified that both shRNAs reduced the expression of Nav1.1 mRNA by around 60% (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; p<0.005 by Sidak's multiple comparisons following ANOVA).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows statistically significant knockdown.

claim: Suppressing Nav1.1 expression using the lenti-shRNAs reduced the INa amplitude in Dlxi1/2b-GFP+ neurons derived from the control hESC line H9.
source: We found that suppressing Nav1.1 expression using the lenti-shRNAs reduced the INa amplitude (Figure 6D middle) in Dlxi1/2b-GFP+ neurons derived from the control hESC line H9
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 6D shows statistically significant reduction.

claim: Suppressing Nav1.1 expression using the lenti-shRNAs did not reduce INa amplitude in CaMKII-GFP+ excitatory neurons.
source: We found that suppressing Nav1.1 expression using the lenti-shRNAs reduced the INa amplitude (Figure 6D middle) in Dlxi1/2b-GFP+ neurons derived from the control hESC line H9, but not in the CaMKII-GFP+ excitatory neurons (Figure 6D left).
evidence: Electrophysiological data in Figure 6D shows no significant effect in excitatory neurons.

claim: The Nav1.1 lenti-cDNA rescued the INa amplitude in the Dlxi1/2b-GFP+ neurons derived from Dravet iPSCs.
